The canteen at the Pune college was nearly empty when Omkar and Swati sat down to prepare for Friday's inter-college debate. Their motion was whether the city should ban private cars from the old market lanes on weekends.
"Shopkeepers will lose customers," Omkar said, tapping his notebook. "Nobody carries heavy bags from a bus stop."
Swati slid her phone across. "The trader association did a count last year. On the two trial Sundays, footfall went up, because families could walk without dodging scooters."
Omkar read it twice. He frowned, then laughed at himself. "That's a fair point. Okay, so my real worry is deliveries, not customers."
He crossed out his first line and wrote: allow early-morning delivery vans.
On Friday, when the other team pushed back, Swati turned to him first. "Omkar, you take the delivery question. They'll believe you."

qa.q: What did the trader association count show about the two trial Sundays?
qa.a: Footfall went up on the two trial Sundays, because families could walk without dodging scooters.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when he read Swati's figures, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was briefly thrown and a little embarrassed, shown by his frown, but then relaxed enough to laugh at himself and accept it rather than defend his first claim.

qa.q: What small habit could help Omkar keep arguing this way in future debates?
qa.a: Before digging in, he could ask himself what his real worry is, as he did with deliveries, so he can drop a weak claim and keep the strong one.

qa.q: How does Swati see Omkar after he changes his position?
qa.a: She trusts his judgement more, which is why she hands him the delivery question on Friday and says the other team will believe him.

grounding: A young adult says that was a fair point, adjusts the argument, and gains a teammate's trust as a result.

"We can't cite this," Nandini said, turning her laptop towards Sarika in the library's group room. "Look, the blog doesn't name a single study."
"It's the clearest explanation of groundwater loss I've found," Sarika said. "And we have to submit by six."
"Clear isn't the same as true. Who wrote it?"
"Someone who runs a water blog. Nandini, it matches what Professor Iyer said."
"Then let's cite what Professor Iyer said. Or the report she mentioned."
Sarika opened her mouth, closed it, and scrolled up. No author page. No references.
"Fine. You're right, and I was just tired. If I'd submitted this and she asked me where the numbers came from, I'd have nothing."
"I'm not trying to win," Nandini said.
"I know. That's why it's easy to say you're right." Sarika opened the university library search. "Give me twenty minutes to find the report."

qa.q: Where were Sarika and Nandini working?
qa.a: They were in the library's group room.

qa.q: Why did Sarika resist Nandini's point at first?
qa.a: Sarika was tired and felt pressured by the six o'clock deadline, and the blog was the clearest explanation found so far, so dropping it felt frustrating.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Sarika checked for an author page and references, admitted Nandini was right, and went to find the report; testing the source rather than defending it protected their project.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini when Sarika concedes?
qa.a: Nandini feels relieved and respected, since the aim was a sound project, not a win, and Sarika's quick agreement shows they are on the same side.

grounding: A student concedes a teammate's better argument about a source and changes course, showing the goal is getting it right.

passage:
I'm Himani, and I still remember the eco club meeting in second year when I was sure I had the perfect plan. I wanted our campus cleanup on Sunday mornings, when the paths are empty and we could work fast.
Mohit listened, rubbed his chin, then said quietly, "Half the volunteers are day scholars. They'd need two buses each way on a Sunday. You'd get the hostel crowd and nobody else."
My face went hot. I had built a whole poster already. For a second I wanted to say the day scholars should just make the effort.
Instead I heard myself say, "That's fair. I planned it around my own timetable."
We moved it to Wednesday lunch. Forty people came instead of the usual twelve. What surprised me more was later: when I proposed the compost pit, nobody argued. Mohit said, "If Himani checked it, it's fine."

qa.q: When did Himani first want the campus cleanup to happen?
qa.a: Himani wanted it on Sunday mornings, when the paths are empty.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when Mohit raised the bus problem?
qa.a: Himani felt embarrassed and defensive, shown by the hot face and the urge to say the day scholars should just make the effort, especially after already making a poster.

qa.q: What could Himani carry forward from this meeting?
qa.a: Before settling a plan, Himani could ask who else it affects, and keep saying so openly when someone points out a gap.

qa.q: How does Mohit see Himani after the meeting?
qa.a: Mohit sees Himani as someone who checks ideas honestly, which is why he backs the compost pit without arguing.

grounding: A young adult concedes a fair point about volunteers' travel, adjusts the plan, and gains credibility for later proposals.

Thursday, late.
Tenzin and I had the fight again tonight. The Bengaluru offer. He says two years there and we'd be settled; I say my team here is finally mine. By nine we were both talking over each other and I heard my voice go sharp in a way I don't like.
Then Tenzin said, "Twenty minutes. Then we come back. Deal?"
I almost said no. It felt like he was dodging. But I was shaking, honestly, so I took my dupatta and walked round the block twice. The chaiwala was closing up. I counted the streetlights.
When I came back, he'd put the kettle on and was sitting at the table, not on his phone. We talked till eleven. Nothing's decided. But we listed what each of us is scared of losing, and his list had my team on it.
Sharmila, you did okay tonight.

qa.q: What did Tenzin suggest when the argument got loud?
qa.a: Tenzin said, "Twenty minutes. Then we come back. Deal?"

qa.q: Why did Sharmila almost refuse the break?
qa.a: Sharmila felt suspicious that Tenzin was dodging the argument, and was also too shaken and angry to trust that a pause would lead anywhere.

qa.q: What made this pause work rather than turn into avoidance?
qa.a: They set a time, Sharmila used it to calm down by walking, and Tenzin was waiting at the table without his phone, so they actually returned to the matter.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt when Sharmila came back?
qa.a: Tenzin was likely relieved and hopeful, since the kettle and the phone-free table show he was ready to listen, and he even listed Sharmila's team as something Sharmila could lose.

grounding: A couple in a heated dispute takes twenty minutes and returns to the matter, showing a planned pause that is not avoidance.

In the kasba, the shop's shutter was half down for the afternoon when Maria and Suraj's argument got loud.
"A whole week closed for your cousin's wedding? The fair is that week," Maria said.
"Every cousin came for our wedding. I can't send a gift and stay behind the counter," Suraj answered.
Their words got faster, and a boy buying matchboxes backed out of the doorway.
Suraj rubbed his face. "Let me take twenty minutes. I'm not running away. I'll come back and we'll finish this."
Maria nodded and went out to the back to water the goats, stamping a little. By the time the bucket was empty her breathing had slowed.
Suraj came back with two glasses of buttermilk from the stall at the corner. They sat on the step.
"Three days," he said. "I go, you open with your brother's help, I'm back before the fair ends."
Maria thought, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Maria do during the twenty-minute break?
qa.a: Maria went out to the back to water the goats.

qa.q: How can you tell Maria was still angry when the break began?
qa.a: She went out stamping a little, which shows lingering anger and frustration even as she agreed to the pause.

qa.q: What did Suraj do that made the pause fair to Maria?
qa.a: He said he was not running away and promised to come back and finish it, then returned with buttermilk and a new three-day plan.

qa.q: What would change if Suraj had walked off without saying he would return?
qa.a: Maria would likely feel dismissed and alone with the problem, and the break would look like avoidance rather than a pause.

passage:
Monday. Farhan asked Manoj why he'd agreed to host his whole office team on Saturday without checking. Manoj sat on the sofa, arms crossed, eyes on the floor. Farhan asked again, louder. Nothing. "Say something!" he shouted, and Manoj walked into the bedroom and shut the door. Farhan slept badly, feeling locked out.
Wednesday. Over dinner Manoj said, "When you get loud, my head fills up. I can't find a single word. It's not that I don't care."
Farhan put down his spoon. "It looks like you've left the room even when you're sitting there."
"I know. I have to be able to tell you when I'm flooding."
The next Sunday, the Saturday plan came up again and voices rose. Manoj uncrossed his arms. "I'm flooding. Back in thirty minutes?"
Farhan breathed out. "Okay. Thirty."
At half past, Manoj came back with a list.

qa.q: What did Manoj do on Monday when Farhan shouted?
qa.a: Manoj walked into the bedroom and shut the door.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling on Monday night?
qa.a: Farhan felt shut out and hurt, locked out of the conversation and then the room, which is why he slept badly.

qa.q: What small step helped them next time?
qa.a: Manoj named what was happening with the words "I'm flooding" and asked for thirty minutes, and Farhan agreed, so the silence became a break with a return.

qa.q: How does Manoj experience the arguments?
qa.a: Manoj feels overwhelmed when voices rise, his head fills up and he cannot find words, so his silence is not coldness but overload.

grounding: A person whose partner goes silent feels shut out and escalates, and they learn a way for the overwhelmed partner to ask for a break.

"The first year I was married, whenever your Mami and I disagreed, she would go quiet. Arms folded, looking at the window. I took it as contempt. So I pushed. I followed her from room to room, repeating myself, louder each time. Once I even banged the steel plate on the table.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?

The rain had turned the highway into a crawl, and Nazia and Jeevan were stuck in the car with an argument that had started at his parents' lunch.
"You let your mother plan our Diwali again," Nazia said. "You didn't even look at me."
Jeevan crossed his arms and stared at the wipers.
"Jeevan. Answer me."
Nothing. The horns outside, the drumming on the roof, and his silence. Nazia's voice rose until she was nearly shouting over the rain. He pressed back into the seat as if she were pushing him.
She stopped. His jaw was tight and he was blinking fast. That wasn't coldness. It looked like too much.
"Are you shutting me out, or is it too much right now?" she asked, quieter.
"Too much," he said, barely. "Can we talk after we're home and I've had a shower?"
"Okay. But we do talk."
He nodded. "We do."

qa.q: What were Nazia and Jeevan arguing about?
qa.a: They were arguing about Jeevan letting his mother plan their Diwali again.

qa.q: Why did Nazia's voice keep rising?
qa.a: Nazia felt ignored and shut out by Jeevan's crossed arms and silence, and the frustration built until she was nearly shouting.

qa.q: What worked in the end, and why?
qa.a: Nazia noticed his tight jaw and fast blinking and asked quietly whether it was too much; that gave Jeevan a way to ask for a break with a clear time to return.

qa.q: What is it like for Jeevan when Nazia gets louder in the car?

passage:
Day one. Deepika's message came at midnight: "You told Amma about my job change before I could." Chaitanya typed back fast, defending himself. She replied in capitals. He replied with a paragraph. By one in the morning there were forty messages, each sharper than the last, and he could feel his sister slipping further away with every one.
Day two. He started a reply at breakfast, then stopped. Every text was making it worse. He pressed call.
"I'm not going to type anymore," he said. "I want you to hear me. I'm sorry. I was excited for you and it came out of my mouth."
There was a long breath on the line. "I wanted to tell her myself, Chaitu."
"I know. That's fair."
Day nine. They met for tea near her office. She talked about the new team; he mostly listened. When she left, she hugged him the old way, tight.

qa.q: How many messages had been sent by one in the morning on day one?
qa.a: By one in the morning there were forty messages.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya worried about as the texts piled up?
qa.a: Chaitanya was worried and hurt that his sister was slipping further away with every sharp message, and felt defensive about what he'd done.

qa.q: What choice worked, and why?
qa.a: He stopped typing and phoned her, so she could hear his apology in his voice, which calmed things in a way the forty messages had not.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel about what Chaitanya had done?
qa.a: Deepika felt hurt and robbed of her own news, because she wanted to tell Amma about the job change herself.

grounding: A person sees a sensitive family matter escalating over texts and switches to a call and then a meeting in person.

passage:
"Hansa, before you hit send on that email, sit down. Let Farhan sir tell you something that happened to me.
"About fifteen years ago, when I was new like you, a colleague called Shubha and I disagreed about who had missed a deadline. We wrote emails. She copied her manager. I copied mine. Every reply got longer and colder. By Friday there were eleven people on that thread, and Shubha and I had stopped saying good morning.
"On Monday, I don't know why, I walked to her desk instead of writing. I said, 'This is getting silly on email. Can we have coffee?' She looked surprised, then tired, then she smiled.
"Over coffee we found it wasn't either of us. The client had changed the date and told only one team.
"That thread, Hansa, cost us a week of misery. The coffee took ten minutes."

qa.q: How many people were on the email thread by Friday?
qa.a: By Friday there were eleven people on the thread.

qa.q: What does Shubha's reaction at her desk suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: Her surprise, then tiredness, then smile suggest she was worn out by the cold thread and relieved that someone had offered to talk face to face.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Farhan sir's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: It was walking to Shubha's desk and suggesting coffee, which moved the matter off email so they could find the real cause together.

qa.q: What was the email week like for Shubha?
qa.a: It was likely stressful and lonely for Shubha, since the thread grew colder and they had stopped even saying good morning.

grounding: An elder recalls a dispute escalating over email and how meeting in person brought back warmth and solved it.

passage:
Shankar was in Dubai, Indu in Kochi, and the family chat about his mother's care had been getting worse all evening. Indu wrote that she was doing every hospital visit alone. Shankar wrote that he sent what he could and couldn't fly home every week. Then Indu typed, "You always have an excuse," and saw him start typing, stop, start again.
She put the phone down. Whatever he sent next would be read wrong; whatever she sent would be worse.
She called instead. The video froze on his face twice, so she switched to voice only, the line crackling.
"Shankar, I don't want to fight in writing. I'm tired, that's all."
A pause, then his voice, softer than any message. "I know. I feel useless here. I hate it."
They didn't solve everything. But they agreed he would call Amma every evening at seven, and Indu would take Sundays off.

qa.q: Where were Shankar and Indu during the argument?
qa.a: Shankar was in Dubai and Indu was in Kochi.

qa.q: Why did Indu decide to stop texting?
qa.a: Indu felt exhausted and worried that anything written next would be read wrong, and that the argument was only growing worse.

qa.q: What could others learn from Indu's choice?
qa.a: When a sensitive family topic turns sharp over text, switch to a call, even a crackly one, so tone and warmth can come through.

qa.q: How was Shankar feeling far away in Dubai?
qa.a: Shankar felt helpless and guilty, saying he felt useless being so far from his mother's care.

grounding: A person recognises a sensitive family matter is escalating over messages and calls, so voice can carry the warmth text cannot.

passage:
On the metro from Andheri, Yash saw the two blue ticks under his message to Dhruv: "Can you pass my CV to your team lead?" Read at 10:14. It was now 11:30.
He scrolled back through the chat as though the answer might be hidden there. Maybe Dhruv didn't think he was good enough. Maybe asking for a referral had been cheeky. Maybe Dhruv was embarrassed to say no. By the time he got off, Yash had half-written an apology for asking.
He didn't send it. Instead he bought a cutting chai and told himself one plain fact: people read messages in lifts, in meetings, in queues, and forget to reply.
At 7:40 in the evening his phone buzzed.
"Sorry yaar, back-to-back client calls all day. Sent your CV at lunch, she wants to talk Thursday."
Yash stared at it, then laughed at the apology still sitting in his drafts.

qa.q: When had Dhruv read Yash's message?
qa.a: The message was read at 10:14.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling as he scrolled back through the chat?
qa.a: Yash was anxious and doubtful, fearing Dhruv thought he wasn't good enough or that asking had been cheeky.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Not sending the apology and reminding himself that people read messages and forget to reply kept him from making an awkward situation out of nothing.

qa.q: What would change if Yash had sent the apology?
qa.a: Dhruv might have felt confused or guilty, and Yash would have made his own request look like a mistake when it wasn't.

grounding: A person sees a message read but unanswered and spins explanations, then finds the delay was busyness.

passage:
"Vaibhav, she's seen it. Look. Seen at nine-thirty."
"Seen what?"
"I told Mala I can't come for her engagement shopping on Sunday. She saw it and said nothing. Three hours!"
"Your sister's at work, Hemant."
"She checks her phone every five minutes. She's angry. Or she's telling Mummy what a useless brother I am."
"Or she's in a meeting."
"You don't know Mala."
"I know you. Last month you thought your manager was going to fire you because she took a day to answer."
"...That was different."
"She promoted you."
Hemant sat down heavily. "Fine. But why read it and not answer?"
"Because she read it in a lift and then the lift door opened. Put the phone in the drawer. Let's eat."
At four, Hemant's phone buzzed. Vaibhav read it over his shoulder: "No problem bhai, come next Sunday then? Busy day, sorry!"

qa.q: When did Mala see Hemant's message?
qa.a: Mala saw it at nine-thirty.

qa.q: What was Hemant afraid Mala was thinking?
qa.a: Hemant was anxious and guilty, afraid Mala was angry and telling Mummy he was a useless brother.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that helped?
qa.a: Vaibhav offered simple, likely explanations, reminded Hemant of the manager worry that proved wrong, and suggested putting the phone away to eat.

qa.q: How did Mala likely see the delay?
qa.a: For Mala it was just a busy day; she wasn't upset and even suggested the next Sunday.

grounding: A person spins explanations when a message is read but not answered, and a friend helps him give the benefit of the doubt.

passage:
I'm Darshan, and this was the week before our band's first gig at the college fest. I sent Ujjwal a voice demo of a song I'd written. Two ticks, blue, at eight in the evening. Then nothing.
I spent the night decoding silence. He thinks the chorus is cheesy. He's telling the others it's not good enough for the fest. He's looking for a polite way to say no. I checked the chat maybe thirty times. Every time the ticks were still blue and the space under them still empty.
Around midnight I made myself write down what else it could be: dinner, homework, his little brother's exam, sleep.
Next morning he came to practice early, humming the chorus.
"Sorry I didn't reply," he said. "I listened to it on loop and then my dad needed the phone."
I've tried, since then, to give people a night before I write their reviews for them.

qa.q: What did Darshan send to Ujjwal?
qa.a: Darshan sent Ujjwal a voice demo of a song Darshan had written.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel through that night?
qa.a: Darshan felt anxious and hurt, afraid Ujjwal thought the chorus was cheesy and would say it wasn't good enough for the fest.

qa.q: What small step helped Darshan, and could help others?
qa.a: Writing down other possible reasons for the silence, like dinner or sleep, gave Darshan a calmer way to wait.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel about the song?
qa.a: Ujjwal liked it enough to listen on loop and hum the chorus, and was a little sorry he hadn't replied.

grounding: A person spins explanations for a read but unanswered message, then learns the delay meant busyness, not rejection.

passage:
Yusuf lay on his bed in the Hyderabad flat, phone close to his mouth, laughing so hard he had to stop the recording twice. Four minutes about the gully cricket match: the ball in Mrs Reddy's balcony, the dog that stole the stumps, his own dramatic slip. He sent it to Rehana, then another two minutes because he'd forgotten the best part.
Rehana was at her aunt's dinner table. The phone buzzed twice. She pressed play under the table, meaning to hear only a few seconds, and Yusuf's laugh blasted out: "And then I fell flat, like a sack of onions!"
Her aunt raised an eyebrow. Her cousins stared.
Later she sent a voice note back, whispering from the balcony. "Your story was the best thing today. But next time, text me 'long voice note, funny, no hurry' first. My aunt now thinks you're a sack of onions."
Yusuf laughed again, then typed the warning for next time.

qa.q: Where was Rehana when Yusuf's voice notes arrived?
qa.a: Rehana was at her aunt's dinner table.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling while recording the voice note?
qa.a: Yusuf was delighted and amused, laughing so hard he had to stop twice, eager to share the funny match with a close friend.

qa.q: What small, kind change did Rehana suggest?
qa.a: She asked him to text a short warning first, like "long voice note, funny, no hurry", so she could choose when and where to listen.

qa.q: What was it like for Rehana when the note played out loud?
qa.a: Rehana felt embarrassed in front of her aunt and cousins, though she still enjoyed the story and felt close to Yusuf 😊

grounding: A teenager sends long laughing voice notes that feel personal, but they assume the friend has time and privacy to listen.

"Seema! Did you hear my voice note?"
"All six minutes of it, Farida."
"And? Wasn't it the funniest thing? The part where the teacher's chair squeaked?"
"It was funny. I laughed. But I played it in the kitchen."
"So?"
"So my phone was on speaker and Mummy was making rotis. She heard the whole bit about you liking Dev from the science club."
"No. No, no, no."
"Yes. She asked who Dev was for ten minutes."
"Seema, I'm so sorry! I just talk and talk when I record, it feels like we're sitting together."
"I know, and I like that. I miss your voice when we don't meet. But maybe put secrets in text, or ask if I'm alone?"
"Deal. Secrets in text. Voice notes only for squeaky chairs."
"And send me the squeaky chair one again. I want to hear it with earphones."

qa.q: How long was Farida's voice note?
qa.a: It was six minutes long.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when she learned Seema's mother had heard?
qa.a: Farida felt embarrassed and sorry, crying "No, no, no" and apologising at once.

qa.q: What small change did the friends agree on?
qa.a: Farida would put secrets in text or check that Seema is alone, and keep voice notes for funny, safe stories.

qa.q: What do Farida's voice notes mean to Seema?
qa.a: Seema enjoys them and feels close to Farida, missing Farida's voice when they don't meet, even though this one caused an awkward moment.

grounding: A teenager's rambling voice notes feel personal and close, but assume the friend has privacy to listen.

passage:
My name is Naveen, and I used to send Rukmini voice notes at night the way other people send full stops. Two minutes, five minutes, once eleven. I'd lie on the terrace and ramble about the maths teacher's new moustache, a song stuck in my head, whether dogs dream. I'd laugh at my own jokes halfway through. It felt closer than typing, like she was right there.
Then one day at the bus stop, Rukmini said, "I love your notes. But I share a room with my two sisters, so I listen in the bathroom with the tap running, at double speed."
I didn't know whether to laugh or hide. Double speed! All my careful pauses!
We worked it out. I still send them, but shorter, and I start with "no rush". She sends a heart when she's heard it, whenever that is.
Sometimes I still send a long one. She says those are her weekend listening.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini listen to the voice notes?
qa.a: Rukmini listened in the bathroom with the tap running, at double speed.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Rukmini explained how she listened?
qa.a: Naveen felt embarrassed and amused at once, not sure whether to laugh or hide at the thought of the careful pauses played at double speed.

qa.q: What change worked for both of them?
qa.a: Naveen kept sending notes but made them shorter and started with "no rush", and Rukmini replied with a heart once she'd heard them.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had her own room?
qa.a: She could enjoy the long notes calmly at normal speed, and they would feel less like a secret squeezed into the bathroom.

grounding: A teenager's long rambling voice notes feel intimate, but assume the friend has time and privacy to listen.

passage:
"Tanuja! Did you listen to my voice note?"
"Mridul, it was five minutes long. I was in Organic Chemistry."
"But it was important!"
"Then I needed it in words. I saw the notification, saw five minutes, and panicked that something was wrong. I couldn't play it with Professor Rao right there."
"Oh. Sorry. It was about the group presentation. Who does which slides."
"Okay, so what's the plan?"
"I take slides one to four, you take five to eight, Aisha does the conclusion."
"That's it? That's two lines!"
"I also talked about the canteen samosas."
"Mridul!"
"Fine. Next time, a text summary first, voice note for the samosas."
"Thank you. I like hearing your voice, honestly. Just not in a lecture."
"Noted. Also, the samosas really were good."
Tanuja shook her head and wrote "slides 5–8" in her notebook.

qa.q: Which slides does Tanuja take?
qa.a: Tanuja takes slides five to eight.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she saw the five-minute note in the lecture?
qa.a: Tanuja felt anxious and stuck, panicking that something was wrong but unable to play it with Professor Rao right there.

qa.q: What small, kind change did they agree on?
qa.a: Mridul will send a short text summary first and keep voice notes for chatty things like the samosas.

qa.q: How did Mridul see the voice note before this conversation?
qa.a: Mridul thought it was an easy, friendly way to share important news and didn't realise the demand it put on Tanuja's time.

grounding: A student cannot listen to a five-minute voice note in a lecture and asks for a text summary; the sender hadn't realised the demand.

passage:
I'm Himani, and it was a Tuesday on the Virar fast local, packed so tight I couldn't lift my arm properly. My phone buzzed. Rajni. A voice note. Four minutes and fifty-eight seconds.
Rajni never sends voice notes unless something big has happened. I stood there, crushed between a woman with a vegetable basket and the door, with no earphones, imagining everything from a breakup to a family emergency. I couldn't play it. I couldn't type properly either.
Finally I managed: "on train, no earphones, all ok?? can you text the main thing?"
She replied: "yes all ok!! just the internship result. I GOT IT."
I nearly cheered in the compartment. Later that evening I listened to the whole note properly: four minutes of screaming, thanking her mother, and describing the interviewer's cat.
I loved it. I just loved it more at home, sitting down.

qa.q: How long was Rajni's voice note?
qa.a: It was four minutes and fifty-eight seconds.

qa.q: What was Himani worried about on the train?
qa.a: Himani was anxious that something big had gone wrong, imagining everything from a breakup to a family emergency.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who receives a long voice note at a bad time?
qa.a: Send a quick text like Himani did, asking if all is okay and asking for the main point, then listen properly later.

qa.q: How did Rajni likely feel while recording the note?
qa.a: Rajni felt thrilled and excited about getting the internship, wanting to share every detail, without thinking where Himani might be 🎉

grounding: A student on a train cannot listen to a nearly five-minute voice note and asks for a text summary of the main point.

passage:
Lab session note, Wednesday
During the second-year titration practical, Pranav's phone buzzed repeatedly on the bench. He checked the screen, winced, and turned it face down. Twice more it buzzed. On a break he showed me, a little embarrassed: three voice notes from his project partner Eshaan, six, five and four minutes long. Pranav said, "I can't listen here, and if I don't reply he'll think I'm ignoring him."
I suggested he text back that he was in lab and ask for a short text of the main point. He did. Eshaan replied within a minute: "Oh sorry! Just need your part of the report by Friday."
Pranav laughed, but looked relieved. Later Eshaan came by the lab door to apologise; he said he hadn't thought about where Pranav might be.
Next step: I will mention in Monday's briefing that phones stay in bags during practicals, and that a short text is kinder in class hours.

qa.q: How long were Eshaan's three voice notes?
qa.a: They were six, five and four minutes long.

qa.q: Why did Pranav wince when he checked his phone?
qa.a: Pranav felt stressed and worried, unable to listen in the lab but afraid Eshaan would think he was ignoring him.

qa.q: What went right after the supervisor's suggestion?
qa.a: Pranav texted that he was in lab and asked for the main point, and Eshaan's short reply solved it in a minute.

qa.q: How did Eshaan see things once he understood?
qa.a: Eshaan felt sorry, realising he hadn't thought about where Pranav might be, and came to apologise in person.

grounding: An adult's note shows a student unable to listen to long voice notes in a lab, and the sender not realising the demand on his time.
